sections.title: Twenty-seven women and a forest
sections.intro_md:
Most people meet Uttarakhand as a road to somewhere holy: Haridwar, Rishikesh, Kedarnath, Badrinath. Or as a weekend in Mussoorie or Nainital. The more interesting story is how a thin strip of steep, poor, beautiful mountain land taught India to argue about forests, dams, roads and who the hills belong to.

Start in Chamoli in March 1974. The men of Reni village had been sent off to the district town to collect compensation money. While they were away the loggers arrived. What the village women did next became the image of Indian environmentalism, and fifty years later the same valley would be hit by one of the disasters that the women had warned about.

spotlights.name: Chipko at Reni
spotlights.spot_it: Village women in shawls with their arms locked around tree trunks, facing men with axes. The word chipko means 'to stick' or 'to hug'.
spotlights.story_md: The fight began over a sports company. In 1973 a village cooperative in Gopeshwar run by the Gandhian **Chandi Prasad Bhatt** asked for its yearly quota of ash trees. The Forest Department refused it ten trees for farm tools, then gave 300 to Simon Company of Allahabad to make **tennis racquets**. Villagers stopped the axemen with drums and slogans. In March 1974, at Reni, the men had been lured away to collect compensation money when the loggers came for 2,500 trees. **Gaura Devi**, a widow who led the village women's group, gathered 27 other women and told the loggers to shoot her first. They held the forest through the night. Uttar Pradesh later banned felling across more than 1,150 square km for ten years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous environmental protest India has produced started as a fight for firewood and jobs, and was won by women.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ash trees for tennis racquets, saved by 27 women with their arms around them.

sections.title: The state in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Uttarakhand is small: **53,483 square km**, about 1.6% of India, a little bigger than Haryana. Census 2011 counted **1.01 crore** people, 20th among states, at 189 per square km; the state expects about 1.2 crore now. It was carved out of Uttar Pradesh on **9 November 2000** as Uttaranchal, the 27th state, and renamed Uttarakhand from 1 January 2007.

It has two halves with separate histories and languages: **Garhwal** in the west and **Kumaon** in the east, with 13 districts between them. It borders Tibet (China) to the north, Nepal to the east, Himachal Pradesh to the west and Uttar Pradesh to the south. About 86% of it is mountain, about 45% is forest, and only about 14% can be farmed. Dehradun is the working capital; Bhararisain near Gairsain is the summer capital; the High Court sits in Nainital.

sections.title: Ice, meadow, forest, plain
sections.intro_md:
Climb north from Haridwar and in about 200 km you pass through almost every climate on Earth. The **Terai and Bhabar** at the bottom are hot plains of sal forest, grassland and elephants. The **Shivalik** hills and the **Lesser Himalaya** above them are the farming belt of terraced fields, oak and pine, where most people live. The **Greater Himalaya** to the north holds glaciers and some of India's highest peaks: Nanda Devi, Kamet, Trishul, Chaukhamba and Panchachuli.

Between the tree line and the snow are the **bugyals**, high summer meadows where herders take sheep and buffaloes. The state has six national parks, including Corbett, Rajaji and the twin UNESCO site of Nanda Devi and the Valley of Flowers. The whole state is in a high earthquake zone, and its steep young slopes slide in every monsoon.

spotlights.name: Nanda Devi
spotlights.spot_it: A twin-summited white wall seen from Kausani or Ranikhet, the higher western peak sharp and the eastern one lower, ringed by a crown of other giants.
spotlights.story_md: At **7,816 m** Nanda Devi is the highest mountain entirely inside India and the 23rd highest on Earth. Before 1808 it was thought to be the highest mountain in the world. It sits inside a ring of a dozen peaks above 6,400 m, so the only way in is the Rishi Ganga gorge, first forced by Eric Shipton and Bill Tilman in 1934. Two years later Tilman and Noel Odell stood on top, the highest summit anyone had reached until 1950. To the people of Garhwal and Kumaon she is not a mountain at all but the goddess Nanda, a daughter of the hills married off to Shiva.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's highest peak is also its patron goddess, and her sanctuary has been closed to climbers since 1983.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess so walled in that it took until 1934 to find the door.

spotlights.name: Valley of Flowers
spotlights.spot_it: A U-shaped glacial valley at about 3,500 m, carpeted in pink, blue and yellow flowers from July to September, with a snow-fed stream down the middle.
spotlights.story_md: In 1931 the British climbers Frank Smythe, Eric Shipton and R. L. Holdsworth lost their way coming back from Kamet and walked into a valley so full of flowers that Smythe wrote a book named after it. Botanists have since listed about **520 alpine plants** in its 87.5 square km, including blue poppies and the cobra lily. In 1939 the Kew botanist Joan Margaret Legge slipped to her death while collecting there; her sister built the small memorial you still pass. The park is only open from June to October. Together with Nanda Devi it became a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in 2005.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's two natural World Heritage meadows, and a living seed bank of Himalayan flora.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lost climbers found it; a botanist died in it; it is open only four months a year.

spotlights.name: Jim Corbett National Park
spotlights.spot_it: Sal forest and wide grassy chaurs along the Ramganga river, with elephants crossing the dry riverbed and safari jeeps lined up at Dhikala.
spotlights.story_md: Corbett was the **first national park in Asia**, created in 1936 as Hailey National Park after the Governor of the United Provinces. It was renamed Ramganga in the mid-1950s and then Corbett, after the hunter who had helped draw its boundaries and who died in 1955. In 1973 it was the first park to come under **Project Tiger**, launched there. The park covers about 521 square km, with about 580 bird species and 50 mammals. The wider Corbett Tiger Reserve has some of the highest tiger densities recorded in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where India's tiger conservation started, and still one of its strongholds.
spotlights.memory_hook: Asia's first national park was named after a governor, then a river, then a hunter.

spotlights.name: Himalayan monal
spotlights.spot_it: A plump pheasant whose male shines in metallic green, purple, copper and blue, with a white rump patch in flight and a crest like a spoon on a stalk.
spotlights.story_md: The male monal looks painted by a jeweller: nine iridescent colours that change as he turns. He lives from about 2,100 m to above the tree line, digging for roots and tubers with a heavy bill, and in winter comes down to the oak and rhododendron forests. Its crest feathers were once worn in caps, and hunting for them cut numbers sharply. Uttarakhand made it the **state bird**; Nepal made it the national bird, the danphe. The easiest place to see one is the road and trail between Chopta and Tungnath at dawn.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's emblem bird, and a sign of healthy high forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine colours, one bird, and it digs for potatoes.

sections.title: Where the Ganga is born
sections.intro_md:
Two of India's great rivers start here. The **Yamuna** rises below Yamunotri in the west. The **Ganga** is assembled from many streams. The Bhagirathi comes from Gaumukh; the Alaknanda gathers the Dhauliganga, Nandakini, Pindar and Mandakini at five sacred confluences, the Panch Prayag, before meeting the Bhagirathi at Devprayag. From there it is the Ganga, and at Haridwar it leaves the mountains for good.

The same steep rivers make the state a hydropower prize. Tehri is the largest of dozens of dams and tunnels, built and planned, and every big flood of the last fifteen years has reopened the argument over how much more the valleys can take. Part of the water that Delhi drinks starts here.

spotlights.name: Gaumukh and the Gangotri glacier
spotlights.spot_it: A grey, rubble-covered snout of ice with a dark cave at its foot, from which the Bhagirathi pours out in a muddy torrent, under the fang of Shivling peak.
spotlights.story_md: The **Gangotri glacier** is about 30 km long and holds over 27 cubic km of ice. Its snout is called Gaumukh, the cow's mouth, and it is the source of the Bhagirathi, the stream Hindus treat as the true Ganga. Pilgrims walk 18 km from Gangotri town to reach it. The glacier is retreating: survey maps show the snout has pulled back more than a kilometre since the 1930s, and photographs from the 1960s show a cave that has since collapsed. Above it lie Tapovan meadow and the peak of Shivling, 6,543 m.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The physical head of India's most sacred river, and one of the most watched glaciers in Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Ganga is born from a cow's mouth that keeps walking backwards.

spotlights.name: Devprayag
spotlights.when: The last of the Panch Prayag
spotlights.spot_it: Two rivers of different colours meeting below a cliff town: the Bhagirathi green and fast from the left, the Alaknanda grey-brown and heavier from the right.
spotlights.story_md: At Devprayag the Bhagirathi and the Alaknanda meet and, from this point on, the river is called the **Ganga**. It is the last of the five sacred confluences on the Alaknanda, the Panch Prayag: Vishnuprayag, Nandprayag, Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag and Devprayag. You can often see a clear line where the two waters run side by side before they blend. The town is the base of the priests, the pandas, of Badrinath, who keep genealogy registers for pilgrim families going back generations.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The exact spot where the Ganga gets its name.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two colours go in, one name comes out.

spotlights.name: Tehri Dam
spotlights.spot_it: A huge sloping wall of rock and earth closing a gorge, with a long blue reservoir stretching behind it between bare hills.
spotlights.story_md: At **260.5 m**, Tehri is the tallest dam in India. It took 28 years to build, from 1978 to 2006, and its 52 square km reservoir drowned the old town of Tehri, capital of the Garhwal kings since 1815, along with dozens of villages. About 1,000 MW of hydropower plus 1,000 MW of pumped storage feed nine states, and Delhi drinks some of its water. The environmentalist **Sunderlal Bahuguna** fasted against it for years, arguing that a giant reservoir in an earthquake zone was a risk. In Hindi they now call the reservoir Tehri Lake and run water sports on it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Power and water for the plains, paid for with a drowned capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A royal town lies under a lake where people jet-ski.

spotlights.name: Har Ki Pauri, Haridwar
spotlights.spot_it: Stone steps packed with people at dusk, brass lamps raised in circles, a clock tower behind, and thousands of leaf-cup lamps floating down a fast channel.
spotlights.story_md: Haridwar is where the Ganga leaves the mountains for the plains, and Har Ki Pauri, 'the steps of Hari', is its holiest ghat. A stone is said to bear Vishnu's footprint. Every evening priests swing multi-tiered brass lamps in the **Ganga aarti** while bells ring and people float diyas on leaf plates. Every 12 years Haridwar hosts the **Kumbh Mela**, with an Ardh Kumbh at six years. On the main bathing day of the 2010 Kumbh, officials estimated about 1 crore people bathed. The water at the steps is actually a canal cut off the river, the headworks of the 1854 Ganges Canal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The gateway of the Ganga and one of the four Kumbh cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: The holiest steps of the Ganga stand on a British irrigation canal.

sections.title: Edicts, temples and two kingdoms
sections.intro_md:
People painted rock shelters near Almora long before any written record. The first document is a rock: Ashoka's edicts at **Kalsi**, about 250 BCE. From the 2nd century BCE the **Kunindas** issued coins here, and at Jagatgram near Kalsi archaeologists found brick altars of horse sacrifices from the 3rd century CE.

From about the 7th century the **Katyuri** kings ruled much of the central Himalaya from the Katyur valley near Baijnath and built the first great stone temples. They also built a rare sun temple at Katarmal near Almora, about three centuries before Konark. When they broke up, two kingdoms took shape. In Kumaon the **Chands** ruled from Champawat and, from 1563, Almora. In Garhwal the **Panwars** united 52 small forts, the garhs, and ruled from Srinagar on the Alaknanda. The two fought on and off for centuries; Garhwal and Kumaon still have different languages, dress and food.

spotlights.name: Ashoka's edict at Kalsi
spotlights.spot_it: A large quartz boulder under a protective shed, its face covered in Brahmi letters, with a small outline of an elephant carved on one side.
spotlights.story_md: Near the meeting of the Yamuna and the Tons, the Mauryan emperor **Ashoka** had his fourteen major rock edicts cut into a boulder about 2,300 years ago. They are in Prakrit, in Brahmi script, and talk about non-violence, care for animals and respect between sects. Edict XIII names Greek kings of the time, Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas and Alexander. An elephant drawn on the rock is labelled *gajatame*, 'the best of elephants', a symbol of the Buddha. It is the clearest early evidence that the Himalayan foothills were part of an Indian empire.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The oldest written document in Uttarakhand, and a message from Ashoka to the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: A rock in Dehradun district names five Greek kings.

spotlights.name: Jageshwar temples
spotlights.spot_it: A cluster of more than a hundred grey stone temples with curved shikharas and wooden canopies, packed together in a deodar forest beside a stream.
spotlights.story_md: In a valley of deodar cedars 36 km from Almora stand **125 temples** in one main group, with more clusters nearby such as Dandeshwar. They were built over about seven centuries, from roughly the 7th to the 14th, by the Katyuri kings and later the Chands, and many have the curved Nagara tower topped by a wooden umbrella roof, a hill touch that sheds snow. Jageshwar is claimed by local tradition as one of the twelve jyotirlingas, a claim most texts give to Aundha in Maharashtra. The Archaeological Survey of India runs a museum on site.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest temple cluster in the central Himalaya, built over seven centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: 125 temples in one wood, and each one wears a hat against the snow.

spotlights.name: Rani Karnavati, the 'Nakti Rani' of Garhwal
spotlights.spot_it: No portrait survives; picture instead the old Garhwal capital of Srinagar on the Alaknanda, where her court sat.
spotlights.story_md: Garhwal was once 52 small fortresses, the garhs that give the region its name. The Panwar kings united them and in 1622 Mahipat Shah moved the capital to Srinagar on the Alaknanda. When he died in 1631 his son was seven, and his widow **Rani Karnavati** ran the kingdom. In 1640 a Mughal army under Najabat Khan invaded. Garhwali tradition says she trapped it in the hills and had the noses of captured soldiers cut off, which earned her the name Nakti Rani, the nose-cutting queen. Mughal chroniclers record the expedition's failure; the nose story is from Garhwali and later European accounts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the few times the Mughals were turned back in the hills, led by a regent queen.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen who sent an imperial army home without its noses.

sections.title: Gorkhas, surveyors and hill stations
sections.intro_md:
The modern map of the state was drawn by a short, brutal occupation and a war. The Gorkhas of Nepal took Kumaon in 1790 and Garhwal in 1803. The East India Company drove them out in 1814 to 1816, kept Kumaon and eastern Garhwal, and handed the rest back to the Garhwal royal line as the princely state of **Tehri Garhwal**.

The British then turned the hills into a place to rest, to recruit and to measure. They built hill stations at Mussoorie, Landour, Nainital, Ranikhet and Almora. They raised the Garhwal Rifles at Lansdowne. The Great Trigonometrical Survey and later the Survey of India ran from Dehradun, and trained hill men from border villages to map Tibet in secret. They also took over the forests for timber and enforced begar, unpaid porter labour, which villagers broke in a famous protest at Bageshwar in 1921.

spotlights.name: The Gorkha conquest and the Treaty of Sugauli
spotlights.spot_it: An 1815 painting of eight Gorkha soldiers in white with curved khukri knives, and a map showing land Nepal gave up.
spotlights.story_md: In 1790 the expanding Gorkha kingdom of Nepal took Kumaon, ending the Chand dynasty. In 1803 it beat the Garhwal king Pradyumna Shah, who died fighting at Dehradun in 1804. Gorkha rule lasted only about a dozen years but is remembered as harsh, with heavy taxes and people sold into slavery. When the Gorkhas pressed on British territory, the East India Company went to war in 1814. At Nalapani near Dehradun about 600 defenders under Balbhadra Kunwar held a fort for a month against several thousand. The **Treaty of Sugauli** of 1816 gave Kumaon and Garhwal to the British, who returned a smaller Tehri Garhwal to the old royal line.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Drew the borders that, with small changes, became the state's borders in 2000.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Company won the war and the Gorkhas won its respect: it started recruiting them.

spotlights.name: Nain Singh Rawat, the pundit who counted his steps
spotlights.spot_it: A 2004 Indian postage stamp shows a turbaned man with a beard, and a map of his route across Tibet.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **Milam**, a Bhotiya trading village below the glacier of that name, Nain Singh spoke Tibetan from childhood. Tibet was closed to Europeans, so the Survey of India trained him in secret at Dehradun. Disguised as a Buddhist pilgrim, he counted every step with a rosary of 100 beads instead of the usual 108, and hid notes in a prayer wheel. Walking a trained 2,000 paces to the mile, he reached **Lhasa** in 1866 and fixed its position and height for the first time. He covered about 1,580 miles of route. The Royal Geographical Society gave him its gold medal in 1877.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the great feats of exploration of the 19th century, done on foot, in disguise, by a man from a Kumaon border village.
spotlights.memory_hook: He measured Tibet with a rosary.

spotlights.name: George Everest's house, Mussoorie
spotlights.spot_it: A long low roofless stone house with tall arched openings on a grassy ridge above Mussoorie, with the Doon valley on one side and snow peaks on the other.
spotlights.story_md: George Everest ran the **Great Trigonometrical Survey** of India, and from 1832 to 1843 he lived and worked at Park Estate above Mussoorie, while the survey had its offices in Dehradun. The survey that measured India's shape from the south tip to the Himalaya was steered from this ridge. Everest never saw the mountain that took his name. It was computed as the highest in the world in 1852 by Radhanath Sikdar, working in the survey's office, after Everest had retired, and named after him in 1865 against his own objection. The Survey of India still has its headquarters in Dehradun.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The hill where the map of India was run, and the home of the man the world's highest peak is named after.
spotlights.memory_hook: Everest lived in Mussoorie and never saw Everest.

sections.title: How a hill state was born
sections.intro_md:
After 1947 Tehri Garhwal joined India, and all of today's state was folded into Uttar Pradesh. The hills felt run from Lucknow by people who did not know them. The region had 22 seats in a UP assembly of over 400, while neighbouring Himachal, with a similar population, had its own assembly of 68. The Uttarakhand Kranti Dal was founded in 1979 to demand a separate state.

The movement exploded in 1994, when UP brought in a 27% quota for backward classes that hill people saw as unfair to them. Police firings at Khatima and Mussoorie that September and at Rampur Tiraha on 2 October killed protesters. Six years later Parliament passed the Uttar Pradesh Reorganisation Act, and the new state was born on 9 November 2000. On 9 November 2025 it marked 25 years with a silver jubilee in Dehradun.

spotlights.name: Rampur Tiraha, 2 October 1994
spotlights.spot_it: A roadside crossing on the Delhi to Dehradun highway, now marked by a martyrs' memorial.
spotlights.story_md: In 1994 thousands of hill people set out by bus for a statehood rally in Delhi. On the night of 1 to 2 October, Gandhi Jayanti, Uttar Pradesh police stopped them at Rampur Tiraha near Muzaffarnagar. Police fired on the crowd, killing several people, and women marchers were assaulted. Earlier that September police had also fired on protesters at **Khatima** and **Mussoorie**. A CBI inquiry and later court cases followed, and some trials were still running in the 2020s. In Uttarakhand, 2 October is remembered as a black day as well as Gandhi's birthday.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The violence turned a long regional demand into a mass movement that made statehood unavoidable.
spotlights.memory_hook: The state was born out of a night on a highway.

sections.title: Dev Bhumi, land of the gods
sections.intro_md:
Hindus call Uttarakhand **Dev Bhumi**, and it holds more of the great Hindu pilgrimages than any other state: the **Char Dham** of Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath; the five Kedars and five Badris; the five Prayags; and Haridwar's Kumbh. The high shrines open in late April or May and close after Diwali, when the gods are carried down to winter seats.

But the state's religion is also intensely local. Every valley has its own gods, like Golu in Kumaon or Mahasu in Jaunsar, who act as judges, landlords and family elders and who speak through mediums in jagar. Sikhs walk to Hemkund, Muslims gather at Kaliyar, Tibetan Buddhists built Mindrolling in Dehradun, and millions of visitors queue at Neem Karoli Baba's Kainchi Dham near Nainital. In 2026 the Char Dham yatra passed 56 lakh pilgrims by October, a record.

spotlights.name: Kedarnath
spotlights.when: Open late April or May to November
spotlights.spot_it: A squat grey stone temple with a pyramid roof and golden finial, standing alone in a high valley at 3,583 m with a wall of snow peaks behind it.
spotlights.story_md: **Kedarnath** is the highest of the twelve jyotirlingas of Shiva, at 3,583 m on the Mandakini, and one of the Char Dham. Legend says the Pandavas built it while chasing Shiva, who hid as a bull and sank into the ground; his hump stayed here. Nobody knows who built the present stone temple, but it has survived avalanches and floods. From November the idol is carried down to **Ukhimath** for six months and the doors stay shut under snow. Pilgrims walk 16 to 18 km from Gaurikund, ride ponies or take helicopters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The holiest Shiva shrine of the Himalaya, and the emotional centre of the 2013 disaster.
spotlights.memory_hook: Shiva's hump, under six months of snow.

spotlights.name: Badrinath
spotlights.when: Open April or May to November
spotlights.spot_it: A brightly painted temple front in red, blue, green and gold, like a gateway, on the bank of the Alaknanda, with hot springs steaming below it.
spotlights.story_md: Badrinath is the Vishnu shrine of the Char Dham and one of the four great pilgrimage seats of India. Tradition says **Adi Shankara** re-established it in the 9th century, recovering the black stone image of Badrinarayan from the river. By a custom that goes back to him, the chief priest, the **Rawal**, is a Namboodiri Brahmin from **Kerala**, more than 2,500 km away. Pilgrims bathe in the Tapt Kund, a hot spring at about 45°C, before entering. The temple's bright facade is unlike any other hill shrine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A daily link between the southern tip of India and its northern border.
spotlights.memory_hook: In the coldest temple town, a priest from Kerala and a bath at 45 degrees.

spotlights.name: Tungnath and the Panch Kedar
spotlights.spot_it: A small dark stone temple with a slate roof on a grassy ridge at 3,680 m, prayer flags around it, and Chandrashila summit just above.
spotlights.story_md: Tungnath is among the **highest Shiva temples in the world**, at 3,680 m. It belongs to the Panch Kedar, five shrines that together hold Shiva's body in the Pandava legend: the hump at Kedarnath, the arms at Tungnath, the face at Rudranath, the navel at Madhyamaheshwar and the hair at Kalpeshwar. The walk from Chopta is only about 3.5 km, so it is the easiest high temple in the state. Another 1.5 km up, Chandrashila at about 4,000 m gives a view of Nanda Devi, Trishul and Chaukhamba.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ties the landscape together: five temples, one body, one story.
spotlights.memory_hook: Shiva's arms on a meadow at 3,680 m.

spotlights.name: Hemkund Sahib
spotlights.spot_it: A star-shaped concrete gurdwara beside a still glacial lake ringed by seven peaks, each flying a Nishan Sahib flag.
spotlights.story_md: At about 4,600 m, Hemkund Sahib is one of the **highest gurdwaras in the world**. The Dasam Granth says that in a former life Guru Gobind Singh meditated by a lake ringed by seven peaks. In the 1930s a Sikh soldier, Sohan Singh, identified this lake as the place, and a small gurdwara was built in 1936. Each May the Indian Army and Sikh volunteers cut through snow to open the path, an act of kar seva. Pilgrims cannot stay overnight at the lake, and about 1.5 lakh come in a season. A 12.4 km ropeway from Govindghat was approved in 2025.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how the state's sacred map is shared by more than one faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gurdwara found by a soldier reading scripture as a map.

spotlights.name: Golu Devta and the temple of bells
spotlights.spot_it: Thousands of brass bells of every size hung in rows along a temple's walls and paths, with written petitions on stamp paper tied among them.
spotlights.story_md: Golu Devta is Kumaon's **god of justice**. In legend he was a Katyuri prince, abandoned at birth by jealous queens, who grew up to judge fairly. People who cannot get justice in court write their case on paper, sometimes on legal stamp paper, and leave it at his temple at **Chitai** near Almora or at Ghorakhal. When the wish is granted they return to hang a bell. The temples are now covered in tens of thousands of bells. He also speaks through mediums in jagar sessions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A working folk court that people still use when official ones fail them.
spotlights.memory_hook: A god who accepts petitions on stamp paper and is paid in bells.

sections.title: Myths, mysteries and what is true
sections.intro_md:
Mountains breed stories, and Uttarakhand has more than its share. Some hold up, some do not. The skeleton lake at Roopkund was explained for decades by a royal pilgrimage caught in a hailstorm; DNA has made it stranger. Locals say a nuclear device lies on Nanda Devi; that one is true. Visitors are told that the Ganga's water never goes bad; it does get polluted downstream, and studies of its bacteria-killing viruses are interesting but not proof of magic.

The Kedarnath boulder that shielded the temple in 2013 is real, though whether it 'saved' the temple or the temple's own mass did is argued. The old claim that the Pandavas built Kedarnath is legend; no one knows who built the present temple. Treat the stories as part of the place, and the evidence as a separate column.

visual.title: Claim, and what the evidence says

data.claim: Roopkund's dead were one royal party killed by hail
data.evidence: Partly myth: at least two groups, about 800 CE and 1800 CE

data.claim: A CIA nuclear device was lost on Nanda Devi

data.evidence: A large rock did lodge behind it and split the flow

data.claim: Nanda Devi was once thought the world's highest peak
Uttarakhand had the last village of India
data.evidence: Renamed: Mana is now officially the 'first village'

spotlights.name: Roopkund, the skeleton lake
spotlights.spot_it: A small, often frozen tarn at 5,020 m in a bowl of scree, with bones and skulls scattered along its edge when the snow melts.
spotlights.story_md: In 1942 a forest ranger found hundreds of human skeletons around a glacial lake below Trishul. British officials first feared they were Japanese soldiers. A local song tells of a king of Kannauj and his party struck down by a hailstorm on the way to Nanda Devi, and skull wounds seemed to fit. Then in 2019 a DNA study of 38 individuals upended it: 23 were South Asians who died around **800 CE**, but 14 had ancestry like people of **Greece and Crete** and died around **1800 CE**, with one person of Southeast Asian ancestry. No one knows why Mediterraneans were there.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A myth tested by genetics, which replaced one mystery with a stranger one.
spotlights.memory_hook: The hailstorm story was right about the hail and wrong about the people.

spotlights.name: The CIA's lost nuclear device on Nanda Devi
spotlights.spot_it: Nothing to see: the device has never been found. Picture the Nanda Devi massif from Kausani instead.
spotlights.story_md: In 1965 the CIA and India's Intelligence Bureau sent climbers to put a nuclear-powered listening device on the summit of Nanda Devi to spy on Chinese missile tests in Xinjiang. Its power source was a **SNAP generator** containing plutonium. A storm forced the team down, and they lashed the device to rocks near Camp IV. When they came back the next spring, an avalanche had taken it. It has never been found. The sanctuary was closed to foreign climbers for years, and fears about plutonium in the Ganga headwaters still come up in the press.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how the Cold War reached the state's holiest mountain.
spotlights.memory_hook: Somewhere under the goddess's snow, a plutonium battery.

sections.title: Masks, swords and songs that wake the gods
sections.intro_md:
The performing arts of the hills grew out of ritual. **Ramman** is masked theatre for a village god; **Pandav nritya** acts out the Mahabharata over days, with dancers possessed by the heroes; **jagar** calls gods into human bodies. Wedding processions in Kumaon march behind **Chholiya** sword dancers. Women dance the **jhora** and **chanchari** in linked circles at fairs, singing songs of spring, separation and work.

The instruments are loud and made for open air: the big **dhol** and small **damau** drums, the curved **turri** and **ransingha** horns, the **hurka** hand drum, and the **masakbeen**, a bagpipe the British brought with the army and the hills adopted. The music carries the region's grief too: songs of men gone to the army or the plains, and of women left behind on the terraces. Kumaon also has its own sung classical-folk Holi, the Baithki Holi, sung sitting down for weeks.

spotlights.name: Ramman of Saloor-Dungra
spotlights.spot_it: Men in carved wooden masks of gods, demons and animals dancing slowly in a temple courtyard to drums, in front of a whole village.
spotlights.story_md: Every spring the twin villages of Saloor and Dungra in the Painkhanda valley honour their village god, **Bhumiyal Devta**, with days of ritual theatre. Episodes from the Ramayana are told through song and dance, alongside local legends and comic scenes with masked characters. Each caste and family has a fixed role: the Bhandaris alone may wear the mask of Narasimha. The whole village pays for it and takes part. In 2009 **UNESCO** listed Ramman as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Theatre as village government: who wears which mask encodes the social order.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Ramayana where your surname decides your mask.

spotlights.name: Chholiya, the sword dance
spotlights.spot_it: Men in white with red turbans and long skirts, swords in one hand and small shields in the other, leaping and clashing in pairs ahead of a wedding party.
spotlights.story_md: Chholiya is the war dance of Kumaon, performed by men leading a groom's procession. Dancers fence with swords and shields in mock combat while a band of dhol, damau, turri trumpets, ransingha horns and the masakbeen bagpipe plays. Faces are painted and expressions fierce. One story says it began when Khas and Rajput weddings were often raided by rivals, so grooms brought armed escorts. Its exact origin is unproven.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Keeps alive the drums, horns and martial movement of Kumaon's past.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wedding that marches in like an army.

spotlights.name: Jagar, waking the gods
spotlights.spot_it: A singer with a hourglass drum (hurka) or the big dhol, singing through the night beside a fire while a person in a trance sways and speaks as a god.
spotlights.story_md: In a **jagar** a singer, the jagariya, sings the ballad of a local god, often with dhol and damau or the hand drum called hurka. The rhythm and story build until the god 'descends' into a person, the dangariya, who shakes, dances and answers questions from the family: why the cattle fell sick, which ancestor is unhappy, who stole what. Golu, Narsingh and the Pandavas are common. The dhol players are traditionally from Dalit communities called Auji or Das, who hold this knowledge and are paid in grain and cash.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The core religious music of the hills, part theatre, part healing, part court.
spotlights.memory_hook: The drummers wake the god; the god speaks through a neighbour.

spotlights.name: 'Bedu Pako Baro Masa' and Narendra Singh Negi
spotlights.spot_it: A bouncy hill tune everyone in Uttarakhand can hum, about wild figs ripening all year and kafal fruit ripening in Chaitra.
spotlights.story_md: *Bedu pako baro masa* is the unofficial anthem of Uttarakhand. Its lyrics, about wild figs (bedu) ripening all year while kafal ripens only in spring, were written by Brijendra Lal Shah and set to music by **Mohan Upreti**, building on a folk tune; it became famous in the 1950s and was played for Nehru. In Garhwal, the voice of the region is **Narendra Singh Negi**, a singer and poet from Pauri who has recorded hundreds of songs since 1974 about migration, soldiers, women's work and politics. One of his albums in 2006 was widely credited with hurting a sitting chief minister.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hill music is how the region talks about its biggest wounds: leaving home and being ignored.
spotlights.memory_hook: A song about figs that every soldier from the hills knows by heart.

spotlights.name: Mola Ram and Garhwal painting
spotlights.spot_it: Delicate miniatures of lovers in moonlit landscapes, slender women with large eyes, soft greens and blues, in the Pahari style.
spotlights.story_md: Painters of the Mughal school came to the Garhwal court at Srinagar in the 17th century. Their descendant **Mola Ram** became the court painter and the best known artist of the **Garhwal school**, a branch of Pahari painting. He was also a poet and wrote a history of the Garhwal kings. His *Abhisarika Nayika*, a woman going to meet her lover through a stormy night, is the classic example. Many of his works are in museums in India and abroad.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that the hill kingdoms ran courts with art as fine as those of the plains.
spotlights.memory_hook: A painter-poet who kept a court's memory in pictures and verse.

sections.title: Houses, rice paste and bamboo
sections.intro_md:
Hill crafts come from what the slope provides: stone, slate, deodar wood, ringal bamboo, sheep's wool, copper. The traditional house is the best of them, with animals below and people above, carved doors, and in Garhwal the earthquake-flexing koti banal walls. Copper is hammered into water pots and vessels by the **Tamta** smiths of Almora.

The women's arts are the ones you see most: **aipan** drawn on every threshold, and the jewellery and wraps that mark a bride as Garhwali or Kumaoni. In the border valleys Bhotiya women weave thick wool carpets, shawls and pankhis on looms at home. Many of these crafts are carried on by Dalit artisan families, the Shilpkars, who were long paid in grain and rarely credited.

spotlights.name: Aipan
spotlights.spot_it: White geometric patterns of dots, lines and lotus shapes, drawn with rice paste on a brick-red ochre ground, on floors, doorsteps and puja seats.
spotlights.story_md: Kumaoni women draw **aipan** on thresholds, courtyards and altars for festivals, weddings and rituals. The base is geru, red earth, smeared on the surface; the design is then drawn in biswar, a paste of soaked rice, traditionally with the last three fingers of the right hand. Each occasion has its own pattern: a chowki for Lakshmi at Diwali, small footprints leading in from the door, a dhuli arghya for a sacred thread ceremony. Aipan now carries a **GI tag** and now appears on nameplates, trays and diaries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday art of the Kumaoni home, and now a craft business for women.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red earth, rice paste and three fingers.

sections.title: Millets, greens and sweets from Almora
sections.intro_md:
Hill food is simple, seasonal and built for hard work in the cold. The staples were millets, **mandua** and **jhangora**, and pulses grown on terraces: black soybean (bhatt), horse gram (gahat), and red rajma from Harsil and Munsiyari. Leafy greens, wild nettles and pumpkins fill the gaps. Cooking is in iron kadhais, with mustard oil, jakhiya and timur, the hill spices.

The sweets are a different story: rich khoya sweets from Almora's bazaar, and **arsa**, a fried rice-and-jaggery cake made for weddings. For a long time millets were seen as poor people's food and gave way to wheat and rice from ration shops. Since the 2023 International Year of Millets they have been rebranded as superfood, and mandua biscuits and jhangora kheer appear on restaurant menus in Dehradun.

spotlights.name: Bal mithai
spotlights.spot_it: Dark brown fudge bars, like chocolate, covered all over in tiny white sugar balls.
spotlights.story_md: Almora's famous sweet is **khoya** cooked with cane sugar until it turns dark brown and chewy, cut into bars and rolled in small white balls of sugar-coated poppy seeds. It is credited to Joga Lal Sah, a sweet maker in Almora's Lal Bazaar from 1865, and it became famous in the early 1900s. Local legend says Kumaoni soldiers carried it to Burma in the Second World War, and one shop advertised: 'we have a branch in Burma too'. Today it is the souvenir everyone carries down from the hills.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The taste most people outside Uttarakhand know from the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chocolate made of milk, wearing a coat of sugar beads.

spotlights.name: A Kumaoni and Garhwali meal
spotlights.spot_it: A steel plate with a dark mandua roti, rice, a green spinach-like curry (kafuli), a dark bean gravy (bhatt ki churkani), potato gutke and a green salt.
spotlights.story_md: Hill food is built on what grows on steep terraces. **Mandua** (finger millet) makes dark rotis; **jhangora** (barnyard millet) makes kheer. **Kafuli** is a thick curry of spinach and fenugreek leaves; **chainsoo** is roasted black gram ground and cooked in an iron pan; **bhatt ki churkani** uses the local black soybean. Kandali, the stinging nettle, is cooked as saag. Everything is helped along by **pisyu loon**, salt ground on a stone with garlic, green chilli and herbs, and by chutney of roasted hemp seed. Millets fell out of fashion and are now coming back as health food.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how the mountains shaped a diet of millets, greens and pulses.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stinging nettles for dinner and salt you grind yourself.

sections.title: A year of fairs
sections.intro_md:
The hill year is marked by sankrantis, the days the sun moves to a new sign, rather than by big pan-Indian festivals alone. In spring, at **Phool Dei**, girls go from door to door scattering flowers on thresholds. **Harela** in July welcomes the monsoon. **Ghee Sankranti** in August is for eating ghee. Garhwal's late Diwali, **Igas**, comes in November.

The fairs are where the hills meet. The **Uttarayani** fair at Bageshwar in January was once the great trading fair with Tibet and the place where, in 1921, villagers threw the begar registers into the river. Almora and Nainital hold **Nanda Devi** fairs each September. In Devidhura, men threw stones at each other at the **Bagwal** on Raksha Bandhan; after a court order, fruit has replaced most of the stones. And every twelve years or so the **Raj Jat** walks the goddess home.

spotlights.name: Harela
spotlights.spot_it: Small baskets of bright yellow-green seedlings grown indoors, which elders cut and place on the heads of family members.
spotlights.story_md: Ten days before **Harela**, families sow five or seven kinds of seeds, maize, wheat, barley, mustard, gram, in small baskets kept in the dark so the shoots come up pale yellow-green. On the day, the start of the monsoon month of Shravan, elders cut the shoots and place them on the heads of the young with a blessing. The state government has turned it into a tree-planting day, with schools and departments planting saplings across Uttarakhand, and it is a public holiday.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An old farming festival that now does duty as the state's environment day.
spotlights.memory_hook: A green crown grown in the dark.

spotlights.name: Nanda Devi Raj Jat
spotlights.spot_it: A long line of pilgrims crossing high meadows behind a ringal canopy and a four-horned ram, in a three-week walk to a lake below Trishul.
spotlights.story_md: The Raj Jat sends the goddess Nanda from her parents' home back to her husband Shiva at Kailash. The procession walks about **280 km** over three weeks through villages, forests and the Bedni Bugyal meadow, past Roopkund to the lake of **Homkund** below Trishul. It is led by a **chausingya khadu**, a ram born with four horns, which is released at the end to walk on alone, carrying offerings. The last full Raj Jat was in 2014. In 2026 the Nauti committee put its yatra off to 2027, while the Kurud temple committee ran its own 'Badi Jat' from 5 September 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest and longest pilgrimage in the central Himalaya, and a living link between Garhwal and Kumaon.
spotlights.memory_hook: A four-horned ram walks off alone into the mountains.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Two facts shape daily life: the slope and the road out. Farms are tiny terraces, and much of the hard work on them, cutting fodder, carrying water and wood, is done by women; their labour force participation in official counts is still only about 22%. Men have left for the army, for hotels and offices in Delhi and Mumbai, and for jobs in the plains, sending money home.

The languages are under pressure too. Hindi is now the first language of about 43% of people. **Garhwali** (about 23%) and **Kumaoni** (about 20%) are spoken at home but rarely written, and UNESCO lists both as endangered. Jaunsari, Bhotiya languages and Raji are smaller still. The state has among the highest shares of Brahmins and Rajputs in India, about 19% Scheduled Castes, and small tribes like the Tharu, Buksa, Jaunsari, Bhotiya and Raji.

spotlights.name: A state of soldiers
spotlights.spot_it: A Garhwal Rifles contingent in Republic Day parade, black-capped and green, or the stone barracks of Lansdowne in deodar forest.
spotlights.story_md: The **Garhwal Rifles** was raised in 1887 and settled at Lansdowne, and the **Kumaon Regiment** is based at Ranikhet. In November 1914 Naik **Darwan Singh Negi** of the Garhwal Rifles won one of the first Victoria Crosses given to Indian soldiers, and Rifleman Gabar Singh Negi won another in 1915. Major **Somnath Sharma** of 4 Kumaon won independent India's first Param Vir Chakra, at Badgam in Kashmir in 1947. One family in many villages has a soldier; a large part of the state's households have drawn army pay or pensions, which is why the hills were once called a 'money order economy'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Military service is the state's oldest steady job and a big part of its identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two of the first VCs and the first Param Vir Chakra came out of these hills.

spotlights.name: The Van Gujjars
spotlights.spot_it: A Muslim herding family in front of a thatched hut of grass and wood in the sal forest, with water buffaloes nearby.
spotlights.story_md: The **Van Gujjars** are Muslim buffalo herders who winter in the Shivalik forests of Rajaji and move up to high meadows of Uttarkashi in summer, walking their herds for weeks. They are vegetarian and sell milk. When Rajaji was declared a national park in 1983 and later a tiger reserve, many families were pushed to resettle outside the forest. They are not listed as a Scheduled Tribe in Uttarakhand, which leaves them with fewer rights to the forests they live in.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A test case for how India balances wildlife parks with forest people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Vegetarian Muslim herders who walk their buffaloes to the snowline.

spotlights.name: The Bhotiya traders of the border valleys

where.label: Munsiyari and the Johar, Darma and Niti valleys

spotlights.spot_it: Women in dark wool dresses with heavy silver and coral jewellery, in front of the five snow peaks of Panchachuli at Munsiyari.
spotlights.story_md: In the high valleys along Tibet, communities grouped as **Bhotiyas**, the Shaukas of Johar and Darma among them, lived by trade. Every summer they crossed passes like Unta Dhura with sheep and goats carrying grain, sugar and cloth to Tibetan markets, and came back with salt, borax and wool. Nain Singh came from this world. The 1962 war closed the border and ended the trade almost overnight. Many families moved down and turned to government jobs, wool weaving and tourism. Villages like Milam are now nearly empty.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A whole economy ended by a war and a closed border.
spotlights.memory_hook: Salt from Tibet paid for a valley's life, until 1962.

spotlights.name: The ghost villages
spotlights.spot_it: Locked stone houses with collapsing slate roofs and terraces gone wild with weeds, no one around.
spotlights.story_md: Leaving the hills, *palayan*, is the state's biggest social wound. The 2011 census counted **1,034** villages with no people. The state's Rural Development and Migration Commission reported in 2018 that **734 more** had emptied since 2011, mostly from Pauri and Almora, and its later updates added more. People leave for jobs, schools and hospitals, and because monkeys and wild boar destroy crops on abandoned terraces nearby. Women and the old are often left behind. Some families now come back to run homestays.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state was made to keep hill people in the hills, and the hills are emptying anyway.
spotlights.memory_hook: Over a thousand villages where only the gods are left.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
The hills have produced soldiers, explorers, activists and writers out of all proportion to their size. Some were born here; some came and stayed. Two chief ministers of Uttar Pradesh, G. B. Pant and Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna, came from these districts, and so did two of independent India's best known security chiefs: General Bipin Rawat, India's first Chief of Defence Staff, and National Security Adviser Ajit Doval, both from Pauri Garhwal.

The cricketer **M. S. Dhoni** grew up in Ranchi, but his family comes from Lwali village in Almora district. The poet Sumitranandan Pant was born in Kausani, where Gandhi wrote on the Gita in 1929. **Ruskin Bond**, born in Kasauli, has written about the hills from Landour since the 1960s. Below are four lives that explain the state.

spotlights.name: Jim Corbett
spotlights.spot_it: A thin man with a moustache and hat, holding a rifle, in old photographs; his stone house at Kaladhungi is now a museum.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Nainital in 1875, **Edward James Corbett** became famous for killing man-eating tigers and leopards. The **Champawat tigress**, which he shot in 1907, was credited with about 436 deaths in Nepal and Kumaon. The Leopard of Rudraprayag terrorised the pilgrim road to Kedarnath for eight years until he killed it in 1926. His 1944 book *Man-Eaters of Kumaon* sold worldwide. He later swapped his rifle for a camera and campaigned to save tigers. He left for Kenya in 1947 and died there in 1955; the park was named after him the next year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The hunter whose books made the world care about Indian tigers.
spotlights.memory_hook: He shot the tigers, then put his name to the place that saves them.

spotlights.name: Bachendri Pal
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling woman in a sari receiving the Padma Bhushan; or at the head of an expedition in down jacket and goggles.
spotlights.story_md: Born in 1954 in **Nakuri** near Uttarkashi, the daughter of a trader who crossed into Tibet, Bachendri Pal had a master's degree and a B.Ed. but turned to climbing. On **23 May 1984**, a day before her 30th birthday, she became the **first Indian woman to stand on top of Everest**, after an avalanche had buried her camp a week earlier. She went on to lead women's expeditions, including the 1993 Indo-Nepali team and a 4,500 km trans-Himalaya trek in 1997, and trained climbers for Tata Steel for decades. She received the Padma Bhushan in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Opened Everest to Indian women and made mountaineering a career for many of them.
spotlights.memory_hook: A day before turning 30, the top of the world.

spotlights.name: Sunderlal Bahuguna
spotlights.spot_it: A thin old man with a long white beard and a white cloth tied round his head.
spotlights.story_md: A Gandhian from Tehri, **Sunderlal Bahuguna** took the Chipko message beyond the hills. His appeal to Prime Minister Indira Gandhi helped win a 15-year ban on green felling in the Uttarakhand hills in 1980. From 1981 to 1983 he walked about **4,870 km** from Kashmir to Kohima to carry the message across the Himalaya. His slogan was 'Ecology is permanent economy'. He then spent years fasting and protesting against the Tehri dam. He died of Covid-19 in May 2021. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 2009.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gave Chipko its national and international voice.
spotlights.memory_hook: He walked the whole Himalaya to talk about trees.

spotlights.name: Govind Ballabh Pant
spotlights.spot_it: A heavyset man with a moustache and a Gandhi cap, on Indian postage stamps and as a statue on Nainital's Mall Road.
spotlights.story_md: Born near Almora in 1887, **G. B. Pant** was a lawyer who defended the Kakori accused, led the Congress in the United Provinces, and in 1937 became its premier. After independence he was the **first Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh**, then Union Home Minister from 1955 until his death in 1961. As Home Minister he oversaw the reorganisation of states by language and pushed Hindi as an official language. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1957. Pantnagar, home of the agricultural university that helped start the Green Revolution, is named after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The hill man who ran the biggest state in India and then the country's interior ministry.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Kumaoni ran Uttar Pradesh long before Uttarakhand left it.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Uttarakhand has more trekking routes and viewpoints than anyone can cover, so choose by season. **April to June** is for the Char Dham, Chopta and Tungnath, and the lake towns. **July to September** is monsoon: the Valley of Flowers is at its best, but roads slide and the Char Dham often closes for days. **October and November** are clear and sharp, the best time for Himalayan views from Kausani, Munsiyari or Binsar. **December to March** brings snow to Auli for skiing and to treks like Kedarkantha.

The classic hill towns are crowded on weekends; the quieter alternatives are Landour above Mussoorie, Lansdowne, Chaukori, and the Har Ki Dun valley in Uttarkashi. Rishikesh is the rafting and yoga capital, and the starting point for every road north.

spotlights.name: Rishikesh and the Beatles
spotlights.spot_it: Suspension bridges over a fast green Ganga, temples with tall towers on the bank, rafts in the rapids, and graffiti-covered meditation domes in a ruined ashram.
spotlights.story_md: Rishikesh is where the Ganga leaves the gorges, and it calls itself the **yoga capital of the world**. In February 1968 the Beatles came to Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's ashram for a meditation course, joined by Donovan, Mike Love and Mia Farrow. They wrote dozens of songs, many of which ended up on the *White Album*. Ringo left after ten days, complaining about the food; Lennon left angrily in April. The ashram was abandoned and taken over by the forest; it reopened in 2015 as the Beatles Ashram, inside Rajaji Tiger Reserve. Lakshman Jhula, the old suspension bridge, was closed to traffic in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where Indian spirituality met global pop culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: The White Album was written in a tiger reserve.

spotlights.name: Mana village
spotlights.spot_it: Stone and wood houses on a slope near the Saraswati river, with a hand-painted sign on a tea stall reading 'India's first tea shop'.
spotlights.story_md: Three km beyond Badrinath, at about 3,200 m, **Mana** is a Bhotiya village of the Marchha people on the old trade route over the Mana Pass to Tibet. Its sign used to say 'last Indian village'; since 2022 the government has called it the **first village of India**. Tourists cross the Bhim Pul, a natural stone bridge over the Saraswati said to have been laid by Bhima, and visit the cave where Vyasa is said to have dictated the Mahabharata to Ganesha. The village moves down to lower valleys in winter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A border village rebranded from last to first.
spotlights.memory_hook: Last village became first village with a change of sign.

sections.title: How it earns
sections.intro_md:
When the state was formed, it was mostly farms, forests and army money orders. Since then a tax-holiday package brought factories to the plains: pharmaceutical, auto and FMCG plants at the SIDCUL estates of **Haridwar**, **Pantnagar** and Selaqui. Manufacturing is now about 26% of the state's output and services about 46%; farming has fallen below 10%, even though most families still farm a little. Per capita income, about ₹2.74 lakh in 2024-25, is well above the national average.

**Tourism and pilgrimage** are the other engine, with about 6 crore visits counted in 2024. Hydropower, horticulture (apples, kiwi, aromatic plants) and government jobs make up much of the rest. The weakness is that almost all of this growth is in three plains districts, Dehradun, Haridwar and Udham Singh Nagar, while the hill districts keep emptying. The state also has one of India's highest unemployment rates.

spotlights.name: Forest Research Institute, Dehradun
spotlights.spot_it: A long red-brick building with white columns, arches and domes, set in vast lawns with the Himalayan foothills behind.
spotlights.story_md: The Forest Research Institute grew from a forest school founded in 1878 and became the Imperial Forest Research Institute in 1906. Its main building, designed by C. G. Blomfield in Greco-Roman and colonial style, opened in 1929. It has a plinth area of about **2.5 hectares** and was listed for a time by Guinness as the **largest purely brick building in the world**. The campus covers 450 hectares and also hosts the academy that trains Indian Forest Service officers. Film crews love it; it has stood in for universities in many Hindi films.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Dehradun is India's forestry capital, and this building is why.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's largest brick building was built to study trees.

spotlights.name: IIT Roorkee and the Ganges Canal
spotlights.spot_it: A white neoclassical main building with columns and a dome, and nearby a broad canal crossing a river on a huge aqueduct.
spotlights.story_md: In 1847 the Lieutenant-Governor James Thomason founded a college of civil engineering at Roorkee to train surveyors for the **Ganges Canal**, which Proby Cautley was building from Haridwar. The canal opened in 1854 and was then the largest in the world; at Roorkee it crosses the Solani river on an aqueduct. The college became Thomason College, then the **University of Roorkee in 1949**, and **IIT Roorkee** in 2001. It is the second oldest engineering institution in India, after Guindy in Chennai.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Engineering education in India began with irrigating the Doab.
spotlights.memory_hook: A college founded to dig one canal.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
The last decade in Uttarakhand has been a race between building and the mountain. The **Char Dham road**, a widening of nearly 900 km of highway to the four shrines launched in December 2016, and the **Rishikesh to Karnaprayag railway**, 125 km with more than 80% in tunnels, are bringing more people faster into fragile valleys. Its Tunnel 8, at 14.57 km India's longest rail tunnel, broke through in April 2025. Ropeways to Kedarnath (12.9 km) and Hemkund Sahib (12.4 km) were approved in March 2025.

The mountain keeps answering: Kedarnath in 2013, Rishi Ganga in 2021, Joshimath in 2023, the Silkyara tunnel later that year, and on 5 August 2025 a flash flood on the Kheer Ganga that buried much of **Dharali** village near Harsil, with dozens missing. Politically, Uttarakhand became the first state to bring a **Uniform Civil Code** into force, on 27 January 2025, including compulsory registration of live-in couples. In 2026 the Char Dham yatra set a new record, and the Nanda Devi Raj Jat split between two committees.

spotlights.name: The Kedarnath flood of June 2013
spotlights.spot_it: A damaged town of broken buildings and boulders around an intact grey temple, with a giant flat rock just behind it.
spotlights.story_md: In mid-June 2013 the monsoon arrived early and collided with a western disturbance, dumping days of extreme rain on the high valleys. On 16 and 17 June the Chorabari lake above Kedarnath burst, and a wall of water and boulders tore through the town at the height of the pilgrim season. More than **5,000** people were declared dead or missing across the state. The temple survived, and a huge boulder that lodged behind it, now worshipped as the **Bhim shila**, is credited with splitting the flow.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The disaster that forced India to rethink building and pilgrimage in the high Himalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: A rock now worshipped for saving a temple.

spotlights.name: The Rishi Ganga flood, February 2021
spotlights.spot_it: Satellite images before and after: a dam site in a gorge filled with grey debris; rescuers at a tunnel mouth.
spotlights.story_md: On a sunny winter morning, 7 February 2021, a huge slab of rock and glacier ice broke off Ronti peak and crashed into the Rishi Ganga valley. The debris flow wiped out a small hydropower plant at **Raini**, the same village where Gaura Devi had hugged the trees, and filled the tunnels of the Tapovan Vishnugad project downstream. More than 200 people died or went missing, many of them workers trapped in the tunnels. Scientists traced it to a rock and ice avalanche on a warming mountain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Showed that hydropower in the high Himalaya faces risks that dams cannot design away.
spotlights.memory_hook: Disaster came back to the Chipko village 47 years later.

spotlights.name: Joshimath sinking
spotlights.spot_it: A crowded town of concrete buildings stacked on a steep slope above the Alaknanda; in 2023 the walls carried wide diagonal cracks.
spotlights.story_md: Joshimath, gateway to Badrinath and Auli and seat of one of Adi Shankara's four mathas, sits on old landslide debris. In early **January 2023** cracks opened in hundreds of houses and roads, water burst from the ground, and the town was declared a disaster-prone zone. Reports counted cracks in more than 800 structures and hundreds of people were moved out. Geologists blamed weak ground, unplanned building, no drainage, and possibly the tunnel of a hydropower project nearby, which the company denied. Construction was halted.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A whole town showing what happens when building outpaces geology.
spotlights.memory_hook: A town built on a landslide started to remember it.

spotlights.name: Silkyara tunnel rescue
spotlights.spot_it: The mouth of a highway tunnel, rescue machines and steel pipes, crowds of workers and officials waiting outside.
spotlights.story_md: On 12 November 2023 part of the Silkyara Bend to Barkot tunnel on the Char Dham road collapsed, trapping **41 workers**. They survived 17 days on food, water and air sent through a narrow pipe, with an endoscope camera showing them alive. A giant American auger drill broke down on steel in the rubble. The last stretch was dug by hand by a team of **rat-hole miners**, men from a banned mining practice, who crawled through a pipe and cleared the final metres. All 41 came out on 28 November.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A national drama that also raised hard questions about tunnelling in fragile hills.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the machine failed, the rat-hole miners dug the last metres.

sections.title: Recap: the state in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. Uttarakhand became a state on 9 November 2000, after a long movement and the police firings of 1994.
2. It has two halves, Garhwal and Kumaon, with different kings, languages and food.
3. Nanda Devi, 7,816 m, is its highest peak and its goddess.
4. The Ganga gets its name at Devprayag and leaves the hills at Haridwar.
5. It holds the Char Dham, the Panch Kedar, Hemkund Sahib and Kaliyar.
6. Chipko began here, over ash trees meant for tennis racquets.
7. Corbett was Asia's first national park and the cradle of Project Tiger.
8. Its soldiers won two of the first Indian VCs and India's first Param Vir Chakra.
9. Its villages are emptying even as tourism and factories grow in the plains.
10. Every big project, dam, road, tunnel or rail line, is a bet against fragile, sliding mountains.

side_dish.title: The pundits: measuring a forbidden country with prayer beads
side_dish.body_md:
In the 1860s the Survey of India had mapped almost all of British India by triangulation, but Tibet was closed to Europeans. Captain Thomas Montgomerie had a solution: train men from the Himalayan border villages, who could pass as traders or pilgrims, to survey it secretly. They were called **pundits**, and their reports went in under code names. Nain Singh of Milam was 'Number 9', and later 'the Chief Pundit'.

The training in Dehradun turned a body into an instrument. Each pundit learned to walk a fixed pace, about 2,000 to the mile, on flat ground, up hill and down. A Buddhist rosary of 108 beads was cut to **100**: he slipped one bead every 100 paces, so one round was 10,000 paces, about five miles. Notes went into the prayer wheel in place of the prayer scroll. Mercury for an artificial horizon hid in a pilgrim's bowl; a sextant went into a false bottom of a trunk. Altitude came from boiling water: water boils at a lower temperature the higher you go, and Nain Singh's thermometer put Lhasa at about 3,420 m, close to the true 3,540 m.

In all he counted about 3,160,000 paces. Others followed: his cousin Kishen Singh, and Sarat Chandra Das, a Bengali, whose reports are said to have inspired Kipling's *Kim*.

The lesson for today: before satellites, data came from disciplined human bodies. A step, a bead and a boiling pot were enough to put a capital on the map.

offline_task.title: Make kafuli and a mandua roti
offline_task.body_md:
Tonight, cook the plainest and most typical hill meal.

**Kafuli (serves 2):** Blanch a big bunch of spinach and a small bunch of fenugreek leaves for 2 minutes, then grind them coarse with 2 green chillies and a little ginger. Heat a spoon of mustard oil in an iron kadhai until it smokes, add a pinch of jakhiya or cumin, a pinch of hing and a little garlic. Add the greens, salt and turmeric, and cook for 5 minutes. Stir in 1 tablespoon of rice flour (or besan) mixed in half a cup of water, and simmer until thick, about 10 minutes. Finish with a spoon of ghee.

**Mandua roti:** Mix 1 cup of finger millet (ragi) flour with a quarter cup of wheat flour and warm water into a soft dough. It cracks easily, so pat it out by hand on a wet palm rather than rolling, and cook on a hot tawa.

Eat it with plain rice and a pinch of salt ground with garlic and green chilli, the hill pisyu loon. Notice how heavy and warm a millet meal is: it was built for a day of carrying fodder up a slope.

best_facts.fact: The Chipko movement started in 1973 when the Forest Department refused a village cooperative ten ash trees for farm tools and gave 300 to a company making tennis racquets.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's most famous forest protest began over sports goods.

best_facts.fact: A 2019 DNA study found that 14 of the skeletons at Roopkund, 5,020 m up in the Himalaya, belonged to people with Greek and Cretan-like ancestry who died around 1800 CE.
best_facts.why_surprising: Mediterraneans died in a Himalayan lake and nobody knows why.

best_facts.fact: In 1965 the CIA and India's Intelligence Bureau lost a plutonium-powered spy device near the summit of Nanda Devi. It has never been found.
best_facts.why_surprising: A nuclear battery may lie in the snow above the Ganga's headwaters.

best_facts.fact: Nain Singh Rawat mapped Tibet in secret by counting his steps on a 100-bead rosary and hiding his notes in a prayer wheel, and fixed Lhasa's position in 1866.
The chief priest of Badrinath, near the Tibet border, is by custom a Namboodiri Brahmin from Kerala.
best_facts.why_surprising: The two ends of India meet in one temple.

best_facts.fact: George Everest lived above Mussoorie for over a decade but never saw the mountain named after him; he objected to the naming.
best_facts.why_surprising: The world's highest peak is named after a man who never saw it and did not want it.

best_facts.fact: Ashoka's rock at Kalsi in Dehradun district names five Greek kings of his time.
best_facts.why_surprising: A boulder in the Doon valley links India to the Hellenistic world.

best_facts.fact: The water at Har Ki Pauri, Haridwar's holiest ghat, flows in a channel that is the head of the British-built Ganges Canal.
best_facts.why_surprising: Pilgrims bathe in an irrigation canal.

best_facts.fact: The Garhwal queen Rani Karnavati turned back a Mughal army in 1640 and, by Garhwali tradition, had the captured soldiers' noses cut off.
best_facts.why_surprising: A regent queen beat an imperial army.

best_facts.fact: The 41 workers trapped in the Silkyara tunnel in 2023 were reached in the end by rat-hole miners digging by hand, after a giant auger machine failed.
best_facts.why_surprising: Old, banned skills beat high-tech machines.

best_facts.fact: By the 2011 census 1,034 villages in Uttarakhand had no one living in them, and another 734 emptied by 2018.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state made for the hill people is losing them.

best_facts.fact: Nanda Devi was believed to be the highest mountain in the world until calculations in 1808 showed Dhaulagiri was higher.
best_facts.why_surprising: The state's sacred mountain once held the world title.

best_facts.fact: Corbett was the first national park in Asia, created in 1936, and Project Tiger was launched there in 1973.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's tiger story starts in Uttarakhand.

best_facts.fact: IIT Roorkee began in 1847 as a college to train engineers for a single project, the Ganges Canal.
best_facts.why_surprising: An IIT was born to dig one ditch.

best_facts.fact: The Forest Research Institute's main building in Dehradun was once listed by Guinness as the largest purely brick building in the world.
best_facts.why_surprising: A building about trees is a record for bricks.

best_facts.fact: The 2021 Rishi Ganga flood hit Raini, the same village where Gaura Devi's women had hugged the trees in 1974.
best_facts.why_surprising: History came back to the Chipko village.

best_facts.fact: The Beatles wrote many of the songs of the White Album at an ashram in Rishikesh that is now inside a tiger reserve.
